1.pericope_label: Do we begin again to commend ourselves? or need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you, or letters of commendation from you? Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men: Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart.

schools.summary: Set out why the answer works before admiring it: Corinth was a dissolute and abandoned place, a large number there had been converted and a church organised, an event in such a city would be known abroad, and it had all been done under the labour of these men — so the converts are a better testimonial than any letter. Note that a few manuscripts and versions read your hearts for our, a reading Doddridge adopted, and decline to change the text on that authority. Hear the play on the two verbs rendered known and read, the same pair used earlier in the letter, and add that the thing is literally true, professing Christians being the Bible that other men read. Report that letters of commendation are common in the papyri, list the New Testament instances of commending individuals by letter, and call the practice an important element in the organisation of the early church. Reconstruct how the charge of self-praise reached the apostle — Titus had told him what was said at Corinth — and list the passages in the first epistle they had probably seized on. On the writing itself, note that letters were written on papyrus with a reed and a black pigment, that the Spirit here takes the place of the older finger of God from the giving of the two tables, and that three passages stand behind the phrase about fleshy tables: the heart of flesh promised through Ezekiel, the law written on the heart promised through Jeremiah, and the history of the older covenant.

Place the accusers precisely: the complaint came from men grieved to find their own reputation obstructed by his superior excellence, and they had already faulted the earlier letter on the same ground; grant their pretext was plausible, since it is in itself an odious thing to be the trumpeter of one's own praises. Offer two ways to take the plural in the second verse, either of Silvanus and Timothy, so that the boast others carry about on paper these carry in men's consciences, or partly of the Corinthians themselves; and remark that recommendations obtained by dint of entreaty are often granted by favour rather than by judgement. Then pursue the metaphor: Christ is the author and the apostle the instrument, standing in the place of ink and pen, so that calumniators may understand it is with Christ they have to do. Cite Jeremiah and Ezekiel for the promise of a law written on the heart and a heart of flesh given in place of stone. Note also that some read the opening sentence as a statement rather than a question, and that what the church is asked to see is a work of conversion, not a document.

Take the subject to be chiefly the apostle himself, though not excluding Timothy, Titus and Silvanus, and read the opening as a plain question — have I nothing but my own word to recommend me? Then break the figure of the letter into its parts, since Christ dictates, the apostle writes, the hearts of the readers are the substance written on, and the Spirit produces the influence by which the traces are made; the marks are not made with ink but by the Spirit of the living God, and the change wrought within is what shows without. Add an allusion to the commandments written by the finger of God on tables of stone, over against the fleshly tables of the heart, and say that wherever the writer goes he mentions these converts and praises their gifts and graces.

Read the opening as an objection answered before it is made: the apostle anticipates and puts himself the charge others would have urged, that he vaunts himself, and this though he had already used so strong a corrective as the question who is sufficient for these things. Find the manner characteristic — the man is far removed from appearing to say anything great of himself and avoids it even to great superfluity and excess — and note the irony that the objection grew out of his own success in making tribulation look bright and lustrous. Set beside this the sharper tone he takes later in the letter, where the words are full of a kind of pride, necessarily and properly so, while here they are the words of love.

Treat the passage as an apology for seeming to commend himself: he thought it convenient to protest his sincerity because there were some at Corinth who endeavoured to blast his reputation, yet he was not desirous of vain-glory, and he neither needed nor desired verbal commendation or letters testimonial as the false teachers did. Then make the converts themselves the testimonial he most delighted in, written in his heart and open to be known and read of all men; and draw the general note, that there is nothing more delightful to faithful ministers, nor more to their commendation, than the success of their ministry evidenced in the hearts and lives of those among whom they labour. Be careful to add that the apostle assumes nothing to himself, ascribing all to Christ as the author while he and his fellows were but instruments.

debates.question: Who had accused the apostle of self-commendation, and why?

sides.position: Nobody yet; he anticipates the charge before it is made, as is his manner, being far removed from saying anything great of himself
Rivals grieved to find their own reputation obstructed by his superior excellence, who had already faulted the earlier letter on the same ground
Corinthians reported by Titus, who had sneered at passages in the first epistle and at his lack of authoritative letters
Those who endeavoured to blast his reputation, against whom he thought it convenient to protest his sincerity

debates.question: Should the opening sentence be read as a question?

sides.position: Yes, as a denial — do we begin again to commend ourselves? we do not
Some read it without the interrogation, as a plain statement that they do commend themselves, since it is just to maintain one's reputation

debates.question: Who is meant by the plural in the second verse?

sides.position: Silvanus and Timothy, so that what others carry about on paper these carry in men's consciences; or partly the Corinthians themselves
The apostle chiefly, though not excluding Timothy, Titus and Silvanus

debates.question: Is the text our hearts or your hearts?

sides.position: Our, though a few manuscripts and versions read your, a reading Doddridge adopted; there is not sufficient authority to change it
Our: they are written on his heart, and that letter is patent to the eyes of all men

outliers.note: Alone treats the opening as a study in rhetorical management, noticing that the objection grew out of the writer’s own success in making tribulation look lustrous, and setting the affectionate tone here against the deliberate pride he adopts later in the same letter.
Alone reconstructs the channel of the accusation, that Titus had reported what was said at Corinth, and names the specific passages in the first epistle the critics had probably fastened on.

themes: ye are our epistle, written in our hearts
not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables

4.pericope_label: And such trust have we through Christ to God-ward: Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God; Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.

schools.summary: Explain that the trust rested not on letters of introduction from men but on the evidence of God's presence in the work, and that every part of it was traced to Christ, the apostle having no success and no hope of success that did not depend on him. Then handle the disclaimer with care: the word sufficient had not been used of himself at all but was the implied answer to the earlier question who is sufficient for these things, and the Greek has two different prepositions where the English has one, so that a fair paraphrase runs not as though we are sufficient of ourselves to form any estimate as originating with ourselves. Distinguish starting from ourselves from coming out of ourselves, and note the noun for sufficiency occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. On the next verse, argue that the received rendering about able ministers misses the force of the original, since it suggests men of talent inclined to boast, whereas the verb means that God supplied their deficiency and rendered them competent — offer the coinage that God has sufficienced them for the work. Press the missing articles, so the phrase runs of a new covenant, one not of a written letter but of spirit, and find a direct reference to the words at the last supper and to Jeremiah, the idea of spirit coming from Ezekiel. Then define the letter as the whole written code of Judaism, expressly denying that it means the literal sense as against the mystical.

Disclaim merit without pretended modesty, leaving man nothing: if the smallest part of a good work is not ours, and we are not allowed even to think, how foolish are those who arrogate a right to will. Warn that the Latin term used by the old interpreter has misled some into granting man a right apprehension of the mind which, with a little assistance from God, may effect something of itself. Infer the office's magnitude from the fact that no one can undertake it who has not been previously prepared and fashioned for it by God. Then reject the oldest reading of the letter and the spirit — Origen's, that the letter is the grammatical and genuine meaning of Scripture and the spirit its allegorical sense. Say that this exposition has got into general circulation and become the source of many evils, since it licensed men to adulterate the plain sense, and the more audacity anyone had in doing so the more eminent an interpreter he was accounted, so that the ancients played with the sacred word as if it were a ball to be tossed to and fro. Put in its place the reading that the letter is outward preaching which does not reach the heart and the spirit is living doctrine which makes its way to the soul, the two terms referring not to the exposition of the word but to its influence and fruit.

Reduce the disclaimer to its plainest form: not sufficient so much as to think one good thought, much less to convert sinners. Then read the sufficiency positively, noting that the verb answers the earlier question with the same root, and hold that the apostles execute under divine influence what God himself devised. Deny the common misreading of the letter and the spirit, that the Old Testament kills and the New gives life; the old covenant had both its letter and its spirit, its literal and its spiritual meaning, the law was founded on the supposition of the gospel, and its sacrifices, types and ceremonies refer to it. The Jews rested in the letter, which afforded no means of life but killed by condemning every transgressor, and did not look for the spiritual meaning, and therefore rejected the one who was the end of the law.

Apply the distinction between letter and spirit even to the new covenant: able ministers are ministers not merely of the letter, to read the written word or preach the letter of the gospel only, but of the Spirit also, whose accompanying presence makes the difference. Say plainly that resting in the letter of the gospel leaves a hearer no better, since even that will be a savour of death unto death, while the Spirit going along with the ministry gives life spiritual and eternal.

debates.question: What does the disclaimer of sufficiency exclude?

sides.position: Any estimate originating with ourselves; the Greek has two prepositions where the English has one, and the sufficiency flows from God as its source
Everything, down to the power of thinking; if we may not think, how foolish are those who arrogate a right to will
Chiefly the power to invent such a scheme as the gospel, the words meaning properly to find out by reasoning
So much as one good thought, much less the conversion of sinners

debates.question: Is able ministers a sound rendering?

sides.position: No: it suggests men of talent inclined to boast, whereas the verb means that God supplied their deficiency — he has sufficienced us for this work
No, and the fault is traceable: the Latin term passed into Wycliffe's version, though Erasmus proposed otherwise and Tyndale wrote made us able to minister
The point is that the verb answers the earlier question with the same root, so that God has made us sufficient for these things

debates.question: What is the letter that killeth?

sides.position: The grammatical and genuine meaning of Scripture, the spirit being its allegorical sense — Origen's reading, and the source of many evils
Not that at all, but outward preaching which does not reach the heart, the terms referring to the word's influence and fruit rather than its exposition
The whole written code of Judaism as such, not the literal meaning as against the mystical
The letter of the old covenant, which had both a letter and a spirit; the Jews rested in the former and so rejected the end of the law
A distinction that applies to the new covenant too, since resting in the letter of the gospel leaves a hearer no better

outliers.note: Alone traces the rendering he objects to through its manuscript history, from the Latin version into Wycliffe and thence into the received English, noting that Erasmus and Tyndale had both done better; and alone devotes the bulk of his comment to refuting Origen’s letter-and-spirit as an allegorical rule.
Alone applies the letter-and-spirit distinction to the new covenant as well as the old, holding that a minister of the letter of the gospel only leaves his hearers no better off.

themes: not sufficient of ourselves to think any thing
able ministers of the new testament
the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life

7.pericope_label: But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away: How shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious? For if the ministration of condemnation be glory, much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory. For even that which was made glorious had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth. For if that which is done away was glorious, much more that which remaineth is glorious.

schools.summary: Correct the received rendering of the opening clause, which by using two participles creates a false antithesis between written and engraved and loses the thread; it should run engraved in a writing upon stones, the word for writing being the same as the letter of the previous verse, and the verb should be came into being with glory. Picture the apostle taking up his Greek version of the law and reproducing its words. Note that the verb for engraven is used elsewhere of inlaid work on a table sent to Jerusalem by a Ptolemy. Observe that the expected contrast to the ministration of death would have been the ministration of life, and that the other phrase was chosen because the Spirit is the source of life and confers a higher dignity, so that it is the honour of the gospel ministry to be the means by which the Spirit is imparted. Report that many of the better manuscripts read if there be glory to the ministry of condemnation. Then take the eclipse figure — the glory of the law was real but temporary, the moon making a dim light after sunrise, Christ having thrown Moses into the shade — or, alternatively, reproduce the tense found in the Greek Exodus, that which had been glorified has not been glorified, and hear behind it the transfiguration, where Moses and Elijah appear in glory and are surpassed. Note finally that the participle for done away is present: being done away, not done away.

Say that the glory of the law is extinguished when the gospel comes forth, and prove it by the image: as the moon and stars, though not merely luminous in themselves but spreading their light over the whole earth, disappear before the brightness of the sun, so the law however glorious in itself has no glory in comparison with the excellence of the gospel. Draw the consequence for the reader — that we cannot sufficiently prize the glory of Christ which shines forth in the gospel, and that the gospel is foolishly handled, nay shamefully profaned, where the power and majesty of the Spirit do not come forth to view so as to draw men's minds heavenward. Then grant the law its glories at length before turning them: quote the rabbinic saying that there is no glory but the law, and allow that it was glorious in its author, in its promulgation amid thunderings and a trumpet, in its matter and in its properties. Distinguish carefully what is abolished — between the matter of the law and its ministry, and between the law in the hands of Moses and in the hands of Christ — so that what is ceremonial passes and what is moral abides.

Concentrate the admission into an image: the law was full of splendour, the apostle referring to the thunderings and lightnings at its giving, so that the very body of Moses partook of the effulgence and he was obliged to use a veil. Then say that all this glory was to be absorbed as the light of the stars and moon is absorbed in the splendour of the sun, and reduce the point to a sentence — the greater light swallows up the less. Set the two Greek terms against each other, the one that is counterworked and abolished against the one that continues, the law being for a particular time, place and people and the gospel for all times, places and people. Then turn the ministration of condemnation into an argument: ask how the moral law can be that, if it requires no more than a sincere obedience proportioned to our infirm state, since on that supposition it would become the ministration of righteousness instead.

Explain why the argument needed this turn at all: the comparison so far had set stone tables against hearts and a killing letter against a life-giving spirit, but it still wanted the glory of Moses, since nothing in the new covenant was seen with the eyes of the body. That is exactly what made the old seem great, for its glory was perceived by the senses, being visible to bodily eyes even if it could not be approached, while the other is perceived by the understanding, and to weaker hearers the superiority of the second is not clear. So describe the method: faced with the dulness of his readers, the writer proceeds by placing the difference before them in arguments constructed out of what he had already said.

debates.question: Why does the argument turn here to the glory of Moses?

sides.position: Because the comparison still wanted it: the old covenant's glory was perceived by the senses and the new only by the understanding, and to weaker hearers the superiority is not clear
To illustrate in what the superior glory of the gospel consists, and so to show the importance of the ministerial office

debates.question: How should the opening clause be rendered?

sides.position: Engraved in a writing upon stones, since the received version's two participles create a false antithesis between written and engraved and lose the thread
The ten commandments written on stones, a part of the Mosaic institutions put for the whole

debates.question: In what sense has the older glory no glory?

sides.position: As the moon and stars disappear before the sun, though in themselves they light the whole earth
In the tense of the Greek Exodus: that which had been glorified has not been glorified, as at the transfiguration where Moses and Elijah are surpassed
The ministry of the law, not its matter; the law as in the hands of Moses, not as in the hands of Christ
That which is counterworked and abolished, being for a particular time, place and people, against that which continues for all
It is in process of disappearing: the participle is present, being done away rather than done away

outliers.note: Alone turns the ministration of condemnation into a counter-argument, asking how the moral law can bear that name if it requires only a sincere obedience proportioned to our infirmity, since on that supposition it would become the ministration of righteousness instead.

Alone declines the moon-and-sun figure that four others reach for, reproducing instead the tense of the Greek Exodus — that which had been glorified has not been glorified — and hearing the transfiguration behind it.

themes: the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones

12.pericope_label: Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech: And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished: But their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ. But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart.

schools.summary: Take several hundred words over the sense of hope, canvassing Locke, Rosenmuller and Macknight before settling it, then define plainness of speech as the openness which says all, in which there is no reticence or reserve, setting it against the corrupting of the word charged earlier and matching it to the claim to have kept back nothing profitable. On why Moses veiled his face, observe first that he never declared his own purpose and that the Exodus account suggests the dazzling brightness; then offer the other design, that he was to be a kind of type and figure of his own dispensation — or, following the Greek version, that he veiled his face so that they might not see the end, the fading away of a transitory glory, for them the brightness seeming permanent. Explain the verb for blinded as meaning to cover with thick skin and so to petrify, and note that the veil in question is not the identical one but another with the same effect. Press the grammar of the next clause: it should read that the same veil remains in the reading of the old covenant, the fact not being revealed that the covenant is being done away in Christ — and object that referring the words is done away to the veil does violence to a context which applies them throughout to the law, especially since a different word for withdrawing a veil appears in the next verse. Doubt, finally, that the synagogue mantle is alluded to, since its antiquity is unproved and it covered head and ears but not the face.

Sharpen plainness of speech into a contrast with the alternatives on offer: the apostles speak with all imaginable plainness, keeping back nothing, disguising nothing, concealing nothing, and in this they differ greatly from the Jewish doctors and the Gentile philosophers, who affect obscurity and use figures, metaphors and allegories to hide everything from ordinary people, whereas the apostles wish that all may hear and speak so that all may understand. Take the veil on Moses as typical, representing the types and shadows under which his whole dispensation lay. Then assert the synagogue allusion outright: there is an evident allusion to the practice of covering the whole head with the mantle at the reading of the law, and this voluntary usage is an emblem of the darkness on their hearts even in sacred duties. Catch the force of the word for unremoved, which means not so much as folded back to admit a glimmering, and hold that the veil is now not on Moses or his writings but on the reading of them and on the heart of the unbelieving.

State the inference as a duty for preachers: ministers ought not, like Moses, to put a veil upon their faces or darken what they should make plain, and they are much to blame if they do not set spiritual things in the clearest light possible, since the gospel is a more clear dispensation and its things are revealed not in types and shadows. Then note the privilege of those who enjoy the gospel above those who lived under the law, since we may see the meaning of the types by their accomplishment, the veil being done away in Christ, who was the end of the law for righteousness to all that believe.

Refuse the question about Moses' intention as wrongly put, since the apostle is not reasoning about it at all: it was Moses' office to publish the law and there is no doubt he wished its true meaning apprehended by all, he did not deliberately involve his doctrine in obscurity, the fault lay with the people, and being commanded to put a veil between his face and the eyes of the beholders he simply obeyed — nothing here is said to his dishonour. Then explain why the point is raised at all: there was at that time a grievous stumbling-block arising from the obstinacy of the Jews in rejecting Christ, and weak consciences were shaken, doubting whether to embrace one whom the chosen people did not acknowledge; the answer is that their blindness had been prefigured from the beginning, since they could not behold the face of Moses except through a veil. Lay the whole blame on them, and note that the dulness in question belongs to unbelievers exclusively.

debates.question: Why did Moses put a veil over his face?

sides.position: The Exodus account suggests the dazzling brightness, though another design is intimated here, that he should be a type and figure of his own dispensation
So that they might not see the end, the fading away of a transitory glory, which for them seemed permanent
The question is wrongly put: the apostle is not reasoning about Moses' intention, the fault lay with the people, and Moses simply obeyed a command
Typically, to represent the types and shadows under which his whole dispensation lay

debates.question: Is the synagogue mantle alluded to in the reading of the old covenant?

sides.position: Yes: there is an evident allusion to covering the whole head at the reading of the law, an emblem of the darkness on their hearts
Doubtful: it is not clear the usage goes back so far, and even if it does, it covered head and ears but not the face

debates.question: What is being done away in the fourteenth verse, the veil or the covenant?

sides.position: The covenant: applying the words to the veil does violence to a context which uses them throughout of the law, and a different word for unveiling appears in the next verse
The veil, which is taken away in Christ — that is, from the heart of them that truly believe

outliers.note: Alone refuses the question about why Moses veiled his face, holding that the apostle is not reasoning about Moses’ intention at all, that the fault lay with the people, and that Moses in veiling simply obeyed a command, so that nothing here is said to his dishonour.

Alone objects on grammatical grounds that the words is done away belong to the covenant and not to the veil, since the context applies them throughout to the law and a different verb for unveiling appears in the next verse.

themes: we use great plainness of speech
Moses put a vail over his face

16.pericope_label: Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away. Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.

schools.summary: Refer the turning to the nation and read the verse as a promise that the blindness is not permanent, the true sense of their own oracles one day breaking on them with full and irresistible light. Anchor the language in Exodus, where Moses removed the veil whenever he went in to commune with the Lord, and note that the very verb for turn is drawn from the same chapter, as is the verb for taking the veil from around the face. On the identification that follows, concede at once that the words seem inconsistent with the formulated precision of the creeds, which make Lord a predicate of the Spirit but would hardly make the Spirit a predicate of the Lord; answer that the apostle did not contemplate the language of those later formularies, and that to turn to the Lord Jesus was to turn to one whose essential being, as one with the Father, is Spirit, and who is in one sense the Spirit, the life-giving energy set against the letter that kills. Alternatively prefer the proposal that Lord bears the sense it has in the Exodus verse being quoted, and warn against pressing the language unduly, since the Spirit is interchangeably called the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ. Make him also the sum and substance of the older institutions, in whom the figures and types all centre; and define the liberty as freedom of access to God without fear, set against the fear of the people who were afraid to come near.

Object that the passage has hitherto been badly rendered, since interpreters supply Israel where the apostle is speaking of Moses, that is of the law: the law was turned away in another direction when the Jews shut Christ out of it, and it becomes to them a labyrinth until it is brought to refer to its end — and what is said of the law applies to all Scripture, which is twisted and perverted wherever it is not taken as referring to Christ as its one aim. Then reject the metaphysical reading of the next verse outright: the statement has nothing to do with Christ's essence but points to his office, calling him the spirit of the law, which will be living and life-giving only if he breathes into it, as a body joined to its soul is a living man and without it a useless carcase devoid of feeling. Use this to solve the problem the chapter raises acutely, how the praises David heaps on the law — that it converts souls, enlightens the eyes and imparts wisdom to babes — can stand beside the description of a ministry of sin and death; the answer is that the law is one thing animated and another left to itself. Note also that the Lord to whom the heart turns is Jesus, without whom as its end the law is a mere dead letter.

Say that the conversion will be en masse, the whole nation in every place turning to Christ, so that Gentiles and Jews make one fold under one shepherd, and add that the veil goes that very moment, the types and prophecies then seen with the utmost clearness to be fulfilled. Draw out the parallel with Moses, who veiled his face when he spoke to the people and took the veil off when he returned to speak with the Lord. Having taken the word for spirit as the gospel in the earlier verses, keep that sense here, since Christ is the end of the law for justification and the dispenser of the Spirit's gifts. Then read the liberty broadly: not only liberty from Jewish bondage but from the slavery of sin, from its power, its guilt and its pollution — liberty from servile fear, and liberty to behold the glory with open face, the veil itself having been the emblem of slavery.

debates.question: Who or what turns to the Lord?

sides.position: Israel, or the heart of Israel, in a conversion still future
Moses, that is the law, which was turned away in another direction when the Jews shut Christ out of it; the passage has hitherto been badly rendered

debates.question: What does it mean that the Lord is that Spirit?

sides.position: Not that Christ is of a spiritual essence; the statement points to his office, calling him the spirit of the law, which lives only if he breathes into it
That he whose being, as one with the Father, is Spirit, is in one sense the Spirit, the life-giving energy set against the letter
That he is the sum and substance of the older institutions, in whom the figures and types all centre
That the word bears the sense it has in the Exodus verse being quoted, and should not be pressed unduly
That Christ is the gospel spoken of earlier under the same word, being the end of the law and the dispenser of the Spirit

outliers.note: Alone makes the subject of the turning Moses rather than Israel, declaring that the passage has hitherto been badly rendered, and generalises the reading into a rule that all Scripture is twisted wherever it is not referred to Christ as its one aim.

Alone measures the verse against the later creeds, conceding that those trained in their theology would hardly make the Spirit a predicate of the Lord, and resolving it by observing that the apostle did not contemplate their language.

themes: when it shall turn to the Lord
where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty

18.pericope_label: But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.

schools.summary: Establish first who is included: although the chapter has been mainly about the apostles, this declaration plainly covers all Christians as distinguished from the Jews, all of us and not merely ministers. Insist that the relation to what precedes is sequence and not contrast, and paraphrase — we are free, and so have no need to cover our faces as slaves do before a great king; there is no veil on our hearts and therefore none over the eyes with which we exercise spiritual vision, and we stand as Moses stood before the Lord with the veil withdrawn. Then work at the verb for beholding as in a glass. Canvass the renderings, Macknight's reflecting as mirrors, Doddridge's beholding as by a glass, Locke's with open countenances as mirrors reflecting the glory; report that Philo uses the word of beholding as in a mirror, that Plutarch uses the active for reflecting, that Chrysostom takes it the second way, and that either makes good sense. Or argue more narrowly: the middle voice ordinarily means to look at oneself, which is inapplicable here, but Philo supplies the sense wanted when he makes Moses ask to behold the divine form not mirrored in any created thing but in God himself — so we behold the glory, though not yet face to face, but as mirrored in the person of Christ. Note that the verb for changed is the one used of the transfiguration and that the tense is continuous, so that we do not lose the glory as Moses did provided the beholding goes on; and read from glory to glory as a process which begins in glory and will be consummated in glory. Ground the mechanism in ordinary experience, that we are moulded by the persons we associate with and the books we read.

Say you cannot think how it came into the mind of Erasmus to confine to ministers what is evidently common to all believers, and note that the word for all was added precisely to take in the whole body of the church. Allow that the Greek verb bears both senses, quoting the counsel that drunkards and young men should look at themselves in a mirror, but follow the old interpreter in preferring beholding in a mirror; observe that the figure points at once to the strength of the revelation and to our daily progress in it. Spread the verse wider still on the other side, so that it covers not preachers only but every believer, whether Jew or Gentile, greater or lesser, enlightened by the Spirit and converted; and distinguish two things the phrase about the open face may cover, the object beheld being unveiled and the beholder being rid of his darkness.

Take the mirror as the gospel and the illumination as literal in its way: mirrors among the ancients were of highly polished metal, so that in a strong light the face would be greatly illuminated by the reflected beam, and by contemplating the gospel the soul becomes illuminated with a divine splendour, this sacred mirror casting back on the believing soul the image of the one whose perfections it exhibits. Say that the image lost by the fall is here recovered and restored. Then draw the contrast out: Moses saw the glory and his face shone so that he covered it, Israel being unable to bear the reflected light, whereas we behold the glory in the mirror of the word and our faces shine too, yet we do not veil them but diffuse the lustre, which increases as the mind's eye is fixed more steadfastly.

debates.question: Does we all mean the ministers or every believer?

sides.position: Every believer: it is hard to see how it came into the mind of Erasmus to confine to ministers what is evidently common to all
All Christians as distinguished from the Jews, though the chapter has been mainly about the apostles

debates.question: Does the verb mean beholding in a mirror or reflecting as a mirror?

sides.position: Beholding, following the old interpreter, though Greek usage allows both
Beholding as mirrored in Christ, since the ordinary middle sense of looking at oneself is inapplicable and Philo supplies the wanted meaning
Either makes good sense: Philo has the one, Plutarch's active the other, and Chrysostom took it as reflecting
Reflecting, the gospel being the burnished mirror from which the divine glory is cast back on the beholder

debates.question: What does from glory to glory describe?

sides.position: A process which begins in glory and finds its consummation in glory, the phrase being a characteristic way of expressing completeness
A continuous transformation kept up by continuous beholding, so that we do not lose the glory as Moses did
A degree-by-degree increase of the same love, worthy of the Spirit who works it

outliers.note: Alone names an opponent on the question of who is included, expressing surprise that Erasmus should confine to ministers what the added word for all was plainly meant to extend to the whole church.

Alone rules out the ordinary middle sense of the mirror verb as inapplicable and finds the wanted meaning in a passage of Philo where Moses asks to behold the divine form not mirrored in any created thing but in God himself.

themes: with open face beholding as in a glass
